title: Arnett v. Kennedy (1974)
summary: A tenured federal employee may be dismissed for cause after written notice and a chance to answer, with a full evidentiary hearing only after removal, and the statute's efficiency-of-the-service standard is not too vague.
notes:
Key line: Where the grant of a substantive right is inextricably intertwined with the limitations on the procedures which are to be employed in determining that right, a litigant in the position of appellee must take the bitter with the sweet. (Justice Rehnquist, plurality)

Citation: 416 U.S. 134 (1974).

sections.Parties: The appellants were Alvin Arnett, Director of the Office of Economic Opportunity, and other federal officials responsible for the removal of the appellee. The appellee was Wayne Kennedy, a nonprobationary employee in the competitive civil service who worked as a field representative in the Chicago Regional Office of the Office of Economic Opportunity. Other OEO employees joined as plaintiffs to press a First Amendment claim. Daniel Friedman argued for the Government. The National Association of Letter Carriers and other unions filed amicus briefs supporting Kennedy. The case tested the removal procedures of the Lloyd-La Follette Act.
sections.Material Facts: In March 1972 Kennedy was removed from the federal service under the Lloyd-La Follette Act, 5 U.S.C. section 7501, after Regional Director Wendell Verduin upheld written charges in a Notification of Proposed Adverse Action. The most serious charge was that Kennedy had publicly stated, recklessly and without proof, that Verduin and his administrative assistant had tried to bribe a representative of a community action organization by offering a $100,000 OEO grant if he would sign a statement against Kennedy and another employee. The Act permits removal of nonprobationary employees only for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service, requires written notice of the charges, a reasonable time to answer in writing with affidavits, and a prompt written decision, but states that a trial or hearing is not required before removal. Civil Service Commission and OEO regulations added thirty days' advance notice, an oral reply option, and a post-removal evidentiary appeal with full backpay on reinstatement.
sections.Procedural History: Instead of replying to the charges, Kennedy sued in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois for injunctive and declaratory relief, claiming that the Act and regulations denied him procedural due process by not providing a pre-removal trial-type hearing before an impartial official and that the removal standard was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad in regulating employee speech. A three-judge court agreed on both grounds, 349 F. Supp. 863 (1972). The Government appealed directly to the Supreme Court. Argument was heard on November 7, 1973, and the Court decided the case on April 16, 1974, reversing and remanding by a vote of six to three on the judgment. Justice Rehnquist announced the judgment in an opinion joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Stewart.
sections.Issue: Does the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment require that a nonprobationary federal employee, who by statute may be removed only for cause, receive a trial-type evidentiary hearing before an impartial official before he is removed, or is the statutory scheme of written notice, an opportunity to answer, and a full post-removal hearing with backpay sufficient? Second, is the statutory standard permitting removal for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service unconstitutionally vague or overbroad as applied to employee speech, in violation of the First Amendment?
sections.Holding: The judgment is reversed. Six Justices agreed that the Constitution does not require a pre-removal evidentiary hearing for a tenured federal employee and that the Lloyd-La Follette Act's standard is neither vague nor overbroad under CSC v. Letter Carriers. The plurality reasoned that the statute conferring the right not to be discharged except for cause also defined the procedures for determining cause, so the employee's property interest carried those procedural limits with it and due process demanded no more. Justices Powell and Blackmun, and separately Justice White, rejected that reasoning but concluded on a balancing of interests that pre-removal notice and a written response, followed by a full post-removal hearing with backpay, satisfy due process; Justice White would additionally require an impartial decisionmaker at the pre-removal stage.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Rehnquist's plurality opinion held that Kennedy's property interest in continued employment was created by the Lloyd-La Follette Act, which granted job security and, in the same breath, limited the procedures for determining cause. Because the grant of the substantive right was inextricably intertwined with the procedural limitations, a litigant in Kennedy's position must take the bitter with the sweet; the Due Process Clause does not add an expectancy that Congress withheld. The plurality found the post-removal hearing adequate to protect any liberty interest in reputation and held the efficiency-of-the-service standard sufficiently definite given the range of situations it must cover. Justice Powell, joined by Justice Blackmun, agreed on vagueness and overbreadth but rejected the plurality's theory: a legislature that creates a property interest cannot define away the constitutional procedures for taking it. Balancing the employee's interest in continued employment against the Government's interest in efficient administration and its ability to make the employee whole through backpay, Powell found the existing scheme adequate. Justice White likewise rejected the bitter-with-the-sweet reasoning and agreed that a pre-removal trial was not required, but he concluded that due process demands an impartial decisionmaker at the pre-removal stage and that Verduin, the target of the accusation, could not fairly decide the charges against his accuser. Because six Justices agreed the statute survived, the District Court's judgment was reversed, but no single rationale commanded a majority.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: The plurality linked the entitlement to Congress’s chosen procedures; Powell and Blackmun rejected that linkage because constitutional procedure has an independent source.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The competing opinions frame whether the adequacy of procedure is a constitutional question independent of the statute that creates the entitlement.

learning.separateOpinions: Six to three on the judgment. Justice Powell, joined by Justice Blackmun, concurred in part and in the result in part, rejecting the plurality's bitter-with-the-sweet theory but finding the procedures adequate on balance. Justice White concurred in part and dissented in part, agreeing that no pre-removal trial was required but concluding that Verduin's role as decisionmaker denied Kennedy an impartial tribunal. Justice Douglas dissented on First Amendment grounds. Justice Marshall, joined by Justices Douglas and Brennan, dissented, arguing that a pre-termination evidentiary hearing was required and that the statute was overbroad.
